item.title: Steffi – Half an Owl and a Full Moon Rising
item.dc:creator: Henry Ivry
item.content:encoded:
Steffi
Half an Owl and a Full Moon Rising
Dekmantel

Back in 2022, I described how Steffi had been slowly moving away from the house sound she had first made her name with in the early 2010s. Over time, the Dutch producer and Panorama Bar resident had grown more insular, borrowing from the darker sounds she’d heard downstairs at Berghain. Well, the pendulum now seems to have swung back in the other direction, because Steffi is making house again. It began with last year’s Patterns of Vibration (a collaborative LP with longtime collaborator and partner Virginia), and she’s doubled down with her latest full-length, Half an Owl and a Full Moon Rising. Don’t get it twisted though: this is not an album of feelgood nostalgia (though the rave chords on “Acoustics of Space” certainly do have a touch of that). This is a collection of heavy, late-night tunes that channel her years in the electro and techno trenches. “Free from the Matrix,” for example, has the shuffle and dusty Rhodes pads of throwback Chicago house, but she then adds a minor-key melody that is more Binh than Chez Damier. Similar tricks abound throughout the record, from the anxious synth that bounces off the ropes of “The Rolling Wave” to the bleep that sounds like a soon-to-be-disconnected heart monitor on the LP’s title track. It’s still house music, but it’s also a little haunted.

item.title: Pete Swanson & Ilyas Ahmed – Things Left Unseen
item.dc:creator: Ryan Mandelbaum
item.content:encoded:
Pete Swanson & Ilyas Ahmed
Things Left Unseen
Geographic North

Ilyas Ahmed and Pete Swanson have each put out dozens of releases since the early 2000s (both solo and as part of their hugely respected bands, not to mention their countless scattered collaborations), and while it can be said that they approach the guitar from largely opposing angles—Ahmed with the deft meticulousness of an expert rug maker weaving impossibly intricate patterns, Swanson with the raw, barely controlled force of a chainsaw chewing through concrete—a collaboration between the two Portland stalwarts also happens to make perfect sense. On Things Left Unseen, their distinct styles provide deeply contrasting backdrops for one another, but also emphasize the most essential qualities of their respective sounds. Across two sprawling, side-long tracks, skyward-soaring, reverb-drenched guitar notes shimmer with crystal clarity alongside soft washes of noise, the glowing threads of Ahmed’s celestial tones diving through Swanson’s rumbling tectonic distortions like prisms of light being swallowed up by the earth.

item.title: First Floor #331 – The Corporations Are More Patient Than the Cool Kids
item.description: Thoughts on Superstruct’s latest financial filings, plus a round-up of the latest electronic music news and a fresh batch of recommended new releases.
item.dc:creator: Shawn Reynaldo
item.content:encoded:
Superstruct is back in the news this week. According to reports by IQ and The Telegraph, the UK festival conglomerate—which is partially owned by KKR, a private equity giant with financial ties to to fossil fuel extraction, weapons manufacturing, surveillance technology and businesses that operate in Israel and the occupied West Bank—saw its losses and debt climb significantly during 2025, the year that the company was hit with widespread boycotts targeting Boiler Room, Sónar, Field Day, Mighty Hoopla and a litany of other events in its portfolio.

This is good news, right? Maybe.

Increased losses and debts could be taken as a sign of the boycott’s effectiveness—and several outlets and social media commenters have already spun it as such—but it’s important to note that Superstruct’s revenue also increased in 2025. Moreover, the turbulent year likely included a number of one-time costs due to the acquisition and integration of new assets, along with the costs related to dismissing and replacing various staffers who wound up leaving the company. During the last 18 months alone, Superstruct has hired a new COO (Kane Burton), CEO (Alex Mahon) and director of communications (Amber de Botton).

In other words, it’s probably a bit early for the anti-KKR crowd to start celebrating, and it’s definitely too early to declare that the boycott “worked”—or that it shouldn’t be continued and strengthened as Superstruct gears up for the 2027 festival season. The company, for its part, is already (and not surprisingly) projecting positivity; a spokesman was quoted as saying that “2025 was a period of significant change” and that its new management team is “very pleased with the progress and the trajectory the business is on.”

Companies like this bank on even the most ardent critics gradually getting bored and moving on, and considering the microscopic attention span of the general public when it comes to music industry machinations, it likely falls on people who are actually in the music industry to stand up and push back against the continued incursion of private equity and corporate multinationals into the sector.

Will that happen? I personally wouldn’t bet on it, but rather than continuing to stew, I’ll just go ahead and point you toward the remainder of today’s First Floor digest. As always, it’s designed to catch you up on what’s been happening in the electronic music realm during the past week, and if you read on, you’ll find all sorts of news items and suggested reading links, along with a fresh batch of recommended new releases.

Let’s get started.

IN CASE YOU MISSED IT:

Every week, First Floor publishes a long-form piece that’s initially made available to paid subscribers only. But if you’re not part of the paid tier, now’s your chance to see what you missed! The latest piece is now open to everyone, and it’s an article about San Francisco’s Portola festival. Despite the event’s deeply corporate nature, not to mention its ties to a Christian conservative billionaire with a history of donating to right-wing candidates and causes (including many with a specifically anti-LGBTQ+ agenda), this year’s edition was openly welcomed and promoted by portions of the famously left-leaning city’s electronic and independent music scene. And though it’s a San Francisco story, what happened is indicative of a culture in which “underground” has largely become an aesthetic and growing portion of the music ecosystem has stopped even trying to push back against creeping corporate interests.

The paywall on the above article has been temporarily removed for the next 24 hours. If you’d like exclusive first access to future long-form pieces (and unlimited access to the First Floor archives), then please sign up for a paid subscription.

WHAT’S BEEN HAPPENING

A round-up of the most interesting electronic music news from the past week, plus links to interviews, articles and other things I think are worth sharing.

  • New work from Liz Pelly is usually going to be a must-read affair, and last week, the Mood Machine author debuted a new personal newsletter, kicking things off with an essay about the current state of listening, which she describes as “fraught,” and how it fits into a wider “crisis of distraction” that’s being fueled by online content platforms—including the ones devoted to generative AI.

  • Speaking of the Pelly clan, Jenn Pelly has written a must-read feature of her own for The Guardian, in which she lands a rare interview with Liz Harris (a.k.a. Grouper). The two mostly discuss the unexpected return of Harris’ dream-pop trio Helen, but also touch upon the years in her childhood when her family was immersed in a spiritual cult, and spend time discussing the Oregon-based artist’s struggles with streaming scammers who’ve fraudulently uploaded her music.

  • Streaming fraud is so widespread because A) streaming platforms have made only a half-hearted effort to prevent it from happening and B) real consequences for those who attempt to game the system are rare. This week, however, a North Carolina man was sentenced to 18 months in prison in relation to streaming fraud. Michael Smith had pleaded guilty earlier this year to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, but that was after he’d earned more than $8 million in royalties by using thousands of bots to fraudulently stream hundreds of thousands of songs he’d created using AI. (For what it’s worth, he was also ordered to forfeit those royalties as part of his sentence.)

  • Released in June, Tara Clerkin Trio’s Something Good—which landed in First Floor’s Recommended Releases section—has become one of the year’s sleeper standouts, and now the UK group’s namesake has popped up in The Quietus. Talking to journalist Claire Biddles for a new installment of the publication’s Baker’s Dozen series, she highlights 13 albums—many of them from the late 2000s, when she first moved to Bristol—that shaped her life and musical worldview.

OBLIGATORY BOOK MENTION

My first book is out now. It’s called First Floor Vol. 1: Reflections on Electronic Music Culture, and you can order it from my publisher Velocity Press. However, if you’re outside of the UK, I recommend that you either inquire at your favorite local bookshop or try one of the online sales links that have been compiled here.

JUST ANNOUNCED

A round-up of noteworthy new and upcoming releases announced during the past week.

  • In the midst of the pandemic, Skee Mask and North Americans (a.k.a. LA-based ambient guitarist Patrick McDermott) bonded online, not via music, but through video games. That relationship, however, eventually prompted the two to start collaborating, and after McDermott sent over a batch of material—much of which he’d previously discarded—Skee Mask got to work, and the forthcoming FINAL CIRCLE full-length is the end result. The LP is slated to arrive on October 30 via the City Slang label, and ahead of that, the duo have shared a “Mini Mega Mix” which apparently contains portions of every song on the record.

  • Though Slikback and KMRU both originally hail from Kenya, they’ve pursued quite different musical paths, with the former embracing noise and low-end chaos, while the latter leans into ambient expanses and nuanced field recordings. Nevertheless, the two elected to join forces on a new EP, ENEO, which surfaced last week on Bandcamp and is available in full now as a name-your-price download.

  • Sticking to the theme of unexpected collaborations, Hessle Audio co-founder Pearson Sound and Montreal electro chanteuse Marie Davidson have made a new record together. It’s called Heat, and though two versions of the title track are already available here, the full EP—which includes a remix from Autumns—is due to surface on October 30.

  • claire rousay has worked with a bunch of different labels over the years—much of her recent solo output has been issued via Thrill Jockey—but in a newsletter she published last week, the LA-based experimental artist announced that she would soon be launching her own imprint, quality sounds ltd. The new venture’s first offering is a new EP from rousay herself. Entitled on holding, it’s scheduled to drop on October 9 (i.e. tomorrow), but the song “holy sedative” has already been shared.

  • Lorenzo Senni has a new album on the way. Looking to his past for inspiration, he’s titled it All Ages, and the record is said to find the Italian artist exploring experimental trance and rave sounds through the lens of hardcore punk, skateboarding and straightedge culture. The LP’s first single, “Art Life & Skateboarding,” which has already been shared and features both skate legend Chad Muska and straightedge icon Jamie Thomas, speaks directly to that narrative. The complete album, which also includes a guest appearance by Xiu Xiu frontman Jamie Stewart, is going to be released by Warp Records on November 6.

  • Hodge just released his new Big Splash album—look for that in the Recommended Releases section of today’s newsletter—but the Bristol producer has already unveiled plans for a separate EP for the Interdimensional Transmissions label. Inspired by his experiences playing for IT in Detroit, the record is called Magenta Glow, and though it won’t be available in full until November 30, some preview clips have already been shared.

  • Intellitronic is one of many aliases that Drexciya co-founder Gerald Donald has used over the years, but prior to this week, it had only been tied to a single track, “Pixel,” which appeared on a Juan Atkins-curated compilation called Magic Tracks (Deep Detroit Volume Two) back in 1993. Thanks to Glasgow’s Rubadub label, however, “Pixel” is now back in circulation, and is the title track of a new Intellitronic EP—which is out now—that also contains three previously unreleased tunes.

  • Ending an extended period of quiet, the Voam imprint—which is headed up by Blawan and Pariah—will soon be returning to the fray with a new EP from Rhyw. Considering that the Fever AM co-founder’s last contribution to the label was the world-beating Honey Badger EP, anticipation will likely be running high for Piranha Pop, a four-track effort that’s being billed as “music to make your teeth fall out.” Opening number “Suppli Crush” is out now, and the remainder of the record will follow on November 6.

  • Matrixxman has also been laying relatively low during the past year or so, at least when it comes to releasing new music, but this week the techno mainstay announced that he will soon be offering up a new collaborative record with Berlin-based Australian Connor Wall. Entitled Intercept Orlopp, it’s cryptically described as “a statement from the future, to the future,” and though no audio has been shared yet, more details can be found here. The release will be available digitally via Matrixxman’s own The Grid label on October 16.

RECOMMENDED RELEASES

The following is a summary of First Floor’s favorite new releases that came out during the past week or so. You can hear each one individually via the players embedded below, or you can also just head over to this convenient Buy Music Club list if you prefer to listen to them all in one place. And if you’re interested in checking out First Floor’s complete archive of Recommended Releases, you can find that here.

Helen – Linda’s Head (kranky)

… When Helen—the dream pop trio consisting of Liz Harris, Scott Simmons and Jed Bindeman—released their debut The Original Faces in 2015, it was received with both enthusiasm and puzzlement, as its blurry yet upbeat, vaguely surf-infected shoegaze was a decidedly different affair than the somber ambient folk of Grouper. Since then, the record has become something of a cult classic, a perfect aligning of stars few expected to repeat. Eleven years later, however, the Portland outfit have returned with Linda’s Head, an album that feels like finding yourself within an old and nearly forgotten dream. Ryan Mandelbaum [READ THE FULL WRITE-UP]

The Melting Hours – The Melting Hours (Beyond Space and Time)

The Melting Hours first saw the light of day back in September 2025, when Wata Igarashi and synth wizard Kuniyuki were tasked with warming up Draaimolen’s revered Moon stage. The Tilburg festival has proven to be a fertile laboratory for unlikely B2B experiments, as its organizers intentionally bring together artists, often from different musical orbits, and put them in conversation in front of an expectant crowd. Many of those conversations are one-time-only events, but the Japanese duo discovered a genuine sense of synergy, one that they’ve now funneled into their self-titled debut EP. Offering three tracks of immersive, new age-adjacent transcendence, the record opens with “Blue Sun,” its gentle echoes and lush, crystalline synth evoking the freshness of a misty, dewy morning as they drift in a soft, shimmering ambience. “Liquid Dunes” and “Cloud Touch” go a notch deeper; layers of tinkling water and exotic flute stutters enhance the meditative effect of the former, while the latter elevates into a blissful flow state, its sublime, acidic strings twisting over rhythmically chugging drums. Asmi Shetty

worriedaboutsatan – Outland (Constellation Tatsu)

worriedaboutsatan has been around for 20 years and gone through several different phases, expanding from a solo project to a duo and then shrinking back down to something that UK artist Gavin Miller does on his own. In that time, he’s also amassed quite the resume, but listening to the new Outland album, it makes a lot of sense that his music has previously appeared in the Adam Curtis films Hypernormalisation and Can’t Get You out of My Head. Miller has a real knack for lustrous gloom (or perhaps it’s ominous beauty), and whether he’s crafting moody, post-punk instrumentals (“Isogloss”), billowing slices of ambient trance (“A New Life Awaits You in the Offline Communities”), ponderous trip-hop experiments (“Ancestral Hell”) or quietly cinematic chuggers that stretch past the 13-minute mark (“I Am Vanishing into the Trees”), he makes humanity’s slow march toward oblivion sound positively sublime. Shawn Reynaldo

Harmony – Real Love / Inner Space / Elevate (Deep Jungle)

If one were to compile a list of underappreciated OG junglists, Harmony would need to be somewhere near the top of the list. More than three decades have passed since the UK artist first burst onto the scene, and yet he remains one of its most active participants, dropping several releases per month on his Deep Jungle imprint, with somewhere around half of them containing his own productions. His latest is a good old-fashioned bassbin rumbler, and it opens with the furious drum attack, rave-ready diva vocalizations and golden-era vibes of “Real Love.” The energy level goes up even further on “Inner Space,” a bustling, hoover-filled 4x4 cut, but the sparkly “Elevate” closes out the proceedings on more smooth and soulful note, pairing a bevy of R&B vocal clips with a jazzy bassline straight out of the New Forms playbook. Shawn Reynaldo

Hodge – Big Splash (Local Action)

It says a lot about the current state of electronic music that Hodge’s recent adventures in ADHD-addled, DIY home renovation have sparked more conversation than his latest full-length, but Big Splash is a killer collection of pumping, big-room-ready house cuts. And by “big-room-ready,” I don’t mean cheesy. These are robust, rhythm-forward tunes with some serious heft, and the underlying vibe is much closer to vintage Masters at Work than modern-day Ibiza. The LP’s title track is a particularly confident strutter, while both “Remi’s Groove” and the playfully rolling “Rain Walk” inject a welcome bit of carnival / street party energy into the proceedings. Synths don’t play a leading role on Big Splash, but the wonky melodies and electro-funk flirtations of “Moments of Joy” are a genuine delight, and the crystalline chimes of “Cleo’s Song” help to close out the album on a cool and classy note. Shawn Reynaldo

Struktur – Levitation (Maloca)

Levitation could just as easily be called Meditation, as Struktur—a Berlin-based producer who previously made music under the name Σ—has put together a deeply ruminative collection of tunes. Ruminative, however, should not be mistaken for sedate or ambient; this is an album that’s constantly in motion, and whether it’s exploring skittery IDM (“Grounding”), plinky techno (“Disparity”) or reverb-dusted, post-Mo’ Wax beat constructions (“Falling Through”), its creator remains deeply patient, subtly tweaking his loop-heavy compositions to maximize their hypnotic allure. Struktur may be willing to cultivate a little bit of chaos—most notably via the jittery drum patterns and jagged textures that color the three-song procession of “Suspension,” “Uncertainty” and “Gravitational Pull”—but one never gets the sense that he’s anything but fully in control. Shawn Reynaldo

nthng – Last Light of the Sun (topo2)

If you know, you know. nthng has been releasing records for more than a decade, and though the majority of them have flown well beneath the radar, those who’ve bothered to take a listen have been treated to some quietly brilliant, genre-blurring work. topo2—an Amsterdam label that’s demonstrated a true passion for identifying and boosting underappreciated talents—feels like the perfect landing spot for the Dutch producer, and the new Last Light of the Sun album finds him expanding his sound palette well beyond the traditional confines of house and techno. Included are forays into wiggly, Caterina Barbieri-style synths (“I Hear You”), seductive trip-hop (“Many Reasons”) and blissfully weightless, new age-flavored ambient (“Distance”), but much of the LP’s second half is surprisingly spent exploring various strains of drum & bass, from the industrial-tinged, reverb-drenched “Scattered Mind” to the delicate scuttlings of “Orchid” and the downright radiant closer “Flutter.” Anyone wanting some hazy, moderately deconstructed house cuts can find that too—both “(AM) Sleeper” and “Last Light of the Sun” contain plenty of Actress-isms—but if there’s one takeaway from the album, it’s that nthng is one of those artists who, musically speaking, can apparently do just about anything. Shawn Reynaldo

That brings us to the end of today’s First Floor digest. Thank you so much for reading the newsletter, and remember, you can find all of this week’s recommended releases on this handy Buy Music Club list. (If you like them, please buy them.)

Until next time,

Shawn

First Floor is published and overseen by Shawn Reynaldo, a freelance writer, editor, presenter and project manager. Find him on LinkedIn and Instagram—and make sure to follow First Floor on Instagram as well—or you can just drop Shawn an email to get in touch about projects, collaborations or other potential opportunities.

item.title: Underground Acquiescence
item.description: Thoughts on San Francisco’s Portola festival, the state of the “underground” and what happens when independent music scenes fail to stand up to creeping corporate interests.
item.dc:creator: Shawn Reynaldo
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco has spent decades marketing itself as a bastion of peace, love and counterculture, and even now, nearly 60 years after the original Summer of Love, the city is still widely regarded as a progressive stronghold. (The numbers back that notion; only 7.5% of registered voters are Republicans.) Openly reviled by much of the American political right, San Francisco is the spiritual home of the Beat Generation, the birthplace of Burning Man and the city where Harvey Milk became one of the first openly gay elected officials in the United States. More recently, it’s where Kamala Harris started her political career, and it’s still home to Nancy Pelosi, the 20-term congresswoman who in 2007 became the first female speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives. Within San Francisco, however, those last two politicians are routinely pilloried by left-leaning voters—or at least a sizable percentage of them—for not being nearly progressive enough, which speaks not only to the city’s radical reputation, but how its residents like to see themselves and the place they call home.

As entrenched as that view may be, it’s tough to square with the fact that San Francisco has also long been a magnet for opportunists, con men and nakedly capitalist ambition. The place first blossomed as a literal boom town during the California gold rush, and in the 175 years that followed, it’s experienced repeated—and usually quite sudden—surges of both capital and people, from the massive post-WWII expansion of the defense industry to the ongoing tech explosion that began with emergence of Silicon Valley in the 1980s and 1990s. San Francisco, in other words, has carved out a reputation as a city where fortunes are made, and the mere possibility of striking it rich continues to draw starry-eyed treasure hunters and predatory businessmen alike.

Utopian idealism and unbridled profit-seeking should make for uneasy bedfellows, but in San Francisco, the two camps have forged a kind of truce, with the former dominating the rhetoric as the latter defines the day-to-day experience of actually living within the city limits. The dynamics of that truce are fascinating, and as someone born and raised in the Bay Area1, I spent most of my life watching them play out, marveling as a region that has spent so much time signaling its support for the rights of the oppressed and the working classes also built up the highest concentration of billionaires in the US.

Looking past that discrepancy isn’t easy, particularly in the face of rising costs—the average rent for a San Francisco apartment currently sits at $4800/month (140% higher than the US national average)—and the 2024 election of Daniel Lurie, a nominally liberal heir to the multibillion-dollar Levi Strauss fortune, as mayor. Yet to some degree, that seemingly intractable conflict always been part of life in the city, even within the electronic music scene, where PLUR-spouting vegans and sleazy hucksters have been sharing the dancefloor for decades. (On occasion, they wind up being the same person.)

In that context, it’s not surprising that Portola, an annual music festival which held its fifth edition just last month, has found such an enthusiastic home in San Francisco. Attracting up to 45,000 people per day and often selling out entirely, it’s not a full-blown EDM event, but the programming does skew toward the more commercial end of electronic music; this year’s headliners included Tiësto, Swedish House Mafia, Robyn and Dog Blood (a.k.a. Skrillex and Boys Noize), and they were joined by not-exactly-underground acts like Fatboy Slim, Four Tet, KETTAMA, Soulwax, Marlon Hoffstadt, HorsegiirL, Overmono, Kelela and many, many others. When someone like Ben UFO, who’s a veritable giant in what might be described as the Resident Advisor universe, is listed in a small font on the second-to-last line of the flyer, it seems pretty clear that appealing to the heads isn’t the festival’s top priority.

Is Portola fun? Having never attended myself, I don’t really know, but I also don’t much care, primarily because it’s owned by Goldenvoice. A veteran “alternative” concert promoter originally founded in Los Angeles, the company is best known for operating giant festivals like Coachella, Stagecoach, Just Like Heaven and Camp Flog Gnaw, though those events represent just a portion of its overall business. Goldenvoice also operates an extensive portfolio of venues throughout California, holds exclusive booking deals with several others and in a press release from earlier this year, was said to promote “over 2000 concerts a year in California, Arizona, Nevada, Hawaii, Alaska and Canada, plus recently added North American tours.”

That press release, as it happens, came not from Goldenvoice, but its parent company AEG, a multinational corporation whose founder and CEO, Philip Anschutz, built his fortune in oil, railroads, telecom, real estate and entertainment and currently has a net worth of $19.3 billion, landing him at #141 on Forbes Real-Time Billionaires list. He’s also a Christian ideologue with an extensive history of donating large sums to right-wing candidates and causes, and though he’s denied accusations that he’s anti-LGBTQ+, tax filings from his charitable organization, The Anschutz Foundation, have indicated otherwise.

One might expect a corporate-owned music festival with documented ties to a right-wing Christian billionaire and anti-LGBTQ+ organizations to be shunned in a supposed queer mecca like San Francisco. Add in dance music’s historical roots in the predominantly Black and brown queer communities of Chicago, Detroit and New York, and an event like Portola ought to be a total non-starter, particularly within the the local “underground” electronic music scene, which has repeatedly presented itself as both a bastion of progressive values and a bulwark against the ongoing gentrification and blandification of the city’s cultural landscape.

The “underground,” however, has shown remarkably little resistance as Goldenvoice has pushed deeper and deeper into San Francisco’s electronic music circuit over the past few years, and when Portola rolled around again last month, a portion of the scene was happy to roll out the red carpet.

Read more

item.title: Helen – Linda’s Head
item.dc:creator: Ryan Mandelbaum
item.content:encoded:
Helen
Linda’s Head
kranky

It’s been five years since the last Grouper album, which officially makes this the longest break that Liz Harris has taken between releases since she debuted the project back in 2005. And while some fans might lament the lack of new solo material since 2021’s Shade, for others the arrival of a new Helen full-length is an occasion that’s every bit as worthy of celebration.

When Helen—the dream pop trio consisting of Liz Harris, Scott Simmons and Jed Bindeman—released their debut The Original Faces in 2015, it was received with both enthusiasm and puzzlement, as its blurry yet upbeat, vaguely surf-infected shoegaze was a decidedly different affair than the somber ambient folk of Grouper. Since then, the record has become something of a cult classic, a perfect aligning of stars few expected to repeat. Eleven years later, however, the Portland outfit have returned with Linda’s Head, an album that feels like finding yourself within an old and nearly forgotten dream.

Where The Original Faces’ nostalgic fuzz carried an air of novelty (the original line-up even credited a fictional fourth member named Helen), Helen’s sophomore album sees the band dropping all pretences, obscuring their influences and zeroing in on a sound that feels more like their own. Following the brief yet emotionally gripping opener “Faraway,” the three-track run of “Starline,” “endless sky” and “Linda’s Head” dip into the foggy, narcotic bliss that colored The Original Faces, but everything here is more refined and more direct. The runtimes are brief—most songs on the LP clock in around the two-minute mark—and the arrangements are sparse, but nothing feels half-baked.

Songs like “Dead Shark” and “black and quiet love” strip things back even further, leaving only Harris’ haunted vocals and an acoustic guitar. (What results is akin to peeking into an alternate reality where Grouper plays more major chords and owns a few less effects pedals.) Much of the album drifts by unintrusively, but the softly crashing and receding “darkblue” serves as a sort of gravitational center, while the disarmingly vulnerable, eight-minute closer “Canyon” acts as the long and slow exhale at the end of the journey. Harris isn’t necessarily known for providing listeners with a soft landing place—they’re more likely to feel shattered at the end of a Grouper album—but if Linda’s Head makes one thing clear, it’s that Helen, now more than ever, is a different project altogether.

item.title: First Floor #330 – Flying out the Door
item.description: A round-up of the latest electronic music news, plus a fresh crop of recommended new releases.
item.dc:creator: Shawn Reynaldo
item.content:encoded:
I’ve got a plane to catch this morning—more on that below—so I’m going to keep today’s intro relatively brief. If you’re here, it’s probably because you’re interested in getting caught up on what’s been happening in the world of electronic music.

Or at least I hope that’s why you’re here, because that’s essentially what the First Floor digest (i.e. the edition of the newsletter that goes out every Thursday) is all about. Below you’ll find a thorough round-up of news items and suggested reading links, along with a healthy batch of recommended new releases. And speaking of recommendations, I’ve also recruited Mexican artist Siete Catorce to drop in with a special guest recommendation, and instead of sharing just one record, he’s decided to highlight three of his favorites.

We’ll get into all of that stuff in a second, but first, I wanted to drop a quick reminder that earlier this week, I republished the full archive of Second Floor, a monthly electronic music column I previously wrote for the now-defunct Nina Protocol platform, which took all of its editorial offline a few months back. There are 13 columns in total, and there’s no paywall on any of them, so if you like long-form examinations of various genres (past and present) and in-depth looks at specific geographical scenes, I’d encourage you to dive right in. There’s almost certainly something in that archive which you’ll enjoy.

Alright, I’m off to the airport. Let’s get started with today’s digest.

FIRST FLOOR x GRASP

I’m guessing that many First Floor readers may not be familiar with GRASP, but it’s an offshoot of the long-running Roskilde festival in Denmark. GRASP, however, is designed to be a “platform for knowledge and networking,” and presents several days of talks, workshops, panel debates and other events designed to focus on the idea of sustainable change.

In that spirit, I’ve been invited to give a keynote talk, which has the somewhat imposing title of The Global Live Music Industry in Transition: How Monopolization Is Shaping the Live Music Sector Worldwide. As you might expect, that talk will touch upon many issues I’ve tackled here in the newsletter, zeroing in on corporate consolidation, its impact on the music ecosystem and what, if anything, can be done to effectively push back. That will be happening on Friday, October 2 (i.e. tomorrow), and later that same day, I’ll also be taking part in a separate discussion called Hope for Independence in a Music Industry Under Pressure, where I’ll be joining a group a panelists sharing their thoughts on “how we can create more sustainable, diverse and resilient music ecosystems in a time of significant structural change.”

The complete GRASP program is here, and if you happen to be in Roskilde tomorrow, please do come down and say hello.

WHAT’S BEEN HAPPENING

A round-up of the most interesting electronic music news from the past week, plus links to interviews, articles and other things I think are worth sharing.

  • Former Resident Advisor editor-in-chief Ryan Keeling has maintained a relatively low profile in the years since he left the company, though he has quietly been steering the editorial ship at Pioneer DJ’s in-house publication, The Bridge, for quite some time. Last week, however, he thrust himself (and his face) back into the journalistic spotlight by launching 2 Million Kicks, a new YouTube channel / Substack in which he’ll apparently be “chewing on dance music” via a series of editorially minded video essays. The first installment, which examines the rise of eclectic, genre-blending DJs over the course of the past 15 years, is out now.

  • With Sasha & Digweed’s seminal Northern Exposure mix CD having just been given an official 30th-anniversary reissue, there’s been a rash of press coverage about the legendary DJ duo and the role they played in bringing progressive house and trance to the masses. I won’t list every single article, but Pitchfork made the record the focus of its latest Sunday Review, tapping Philip Sherburne to go long and really dissect not only the two discs of Northern Exposure, but the album’s place in the wider electronic music canon. It’s a quality read, but those wishing to hear reflections from Sasha & Digweed themselves might prefer to check out Simon Whight’s feature for DJ Mag, in which the two artists discuss how the mix came together in the first place, along with the surprisingly mixed reaction it received—from both the public and the press—upon its initial release.

  • Looking to move the conversation about diversity and representation in electronic music beyond the screechy confines of social media, Attack magazine has begun publishing a four-part feature series in which different industry figures are all given an identical set of questions—and, more importantly, are given the space to answer those questions as thoroughly and thoughtfully as they like. The first piece featured Martha Bolton, the founder of NOT BAD FOR A GIRL, which is a London-based collective and booking agency built exclusively around women and gender-diverse artists. Following that was a second feature with Steven Braines, who heads up the HE.SHE.THEY label, festival and global club night. The series’ final two chapters will presumably drop in the days to come.

OBLIGATORY BOOK MENTION

My first book is out now. It’s called First Floor Vol. 1: Reflections on Electronic Music Culture, and you can order it from my publisher Velocity Press. However, if you’re outside of the UK, I recommend that you either inquire at your favorite local bookshop or try one of the online sales links that have been compiled here.

JUST ANNOUNCED

A round-up of noteworthy new and upcoming releases announced during the past week.

  • The three previous releases from Dave Huismans’ genre-defying ex_libris project have all been enthusiastically gobbled up by dance music heads, and the Dutch artist (who formerly went by 2562 and A Made Up Sound) will soon be issuing a fourth installment. Keeping it simple, the new record is called 004, and it’s being billed as “a tightly focused suite of slowly unfolding, percussive midtempo mosaics.” Huismans will be self-releasing it on October 23, and though no audio has been shared yet, more details about the record can be found here.

  • Bicep released a surprise trio of new songs last week: “Air” (which features SOARR on vocals), “Lemonder” and “Viper” (which includes the vocals of Saskia, and also happens to be a collaboration with veteran producer Clark). All three tracks are available now via Ninja Tune, and they’re accompanied by a three-part short film which is said to celebrate “the uniting spirit of the UK’s free party, rave and soundsystem cultures.”

  • Mor Elian and Gramrcy are both busy to begin with. (Aside from DJing and making music, the former runs the Fever AM label alongside Rhyw, while the latter heads up the Peach Discs imprint with Shanti Celeste.) Even so, the two Berlin-based artists have come together to form a new endeavor, one which they say is “built on first-thought-best-thought intuition and calibrated for both immersive listening environments and the physical dynamics of the dancefloor.” The musical component of that endeavor is called a~lo, and the project is set to debut with a self-titled EP that the duo will be issuing via their own newly minted imprint, Bode. No songs from the record have been shared just yet, but some preview clips can be heard over at Juno, which has the EP listed for a November 2 release.

  • No matter how long Jubilee lives in NYC, her heart—or at least a sizable chunk of it—will forever remain in Miami, and that passion comes through loud and clear on the latest release from her Magic City label, which comes from fellow Floridian raver SEL.6. Entitled EXIT 103, the record includes a remix from yet another Miami mainstay, Jonny from Space, and the whole thing is available in full now.

SIETE CATORCE HAS BETTER TASTE THAN I DO

First Floor is in many ways a one-person operation, but each week, the newsletter cedes the spotlight to an artist, writer or other figure from the music world, inviting them to recommend a piece of music.

Today’s recommendation comes from Siete Catorce, a Mexican artist who’s now spent more than a decade crafting hybrid Latin rhythms. Born in Mexicali, he spent much of his early life shuttling between the San Francisco Bay Area and the borderlands of Northern Mexico, and that dual existence fostered a musical upbringing in which hip-hop and dubstep ultimately played as big of a role as regional Latin sounds. Connecting the dots between those genres has always been a part of his work, and long before anyone uttered the phrase “Latin club,” he was turning out his own adventurous permutations… [READ MORE ABOUT SIETE CATORCE + CHECK OUT HIS GUEST RECOMMENDATION]

RECOMMENDED RELEASES

The following is a summary of First Floor’s favorite new releases that came out during the past week or so. You can hear each one individually via the players embedded below, or you can also just head over to this convenient Buy Music Club list if you prefer to listen to them all in one place.

sts – Distant Shapes / Aquifer (STEMcell)

The STEMcell imprint only launched a little more than a year ago, but in that time, its releases have all come from artists working semi-anonymously, adopting aliases that also happen to be the names of stars. Detroit-based upstart sts, however, has thrown that convention aside, maintaining his usual artist moniker while using Distant Shapes / Aquifer to flex his sound design muscles. “Distant Shapes” is an exercise in low-end heft, a sinister, deconstructed dubstep tune with smacking drums that sound like a procession of doors being slammed shut. The second song, “Aquifier,” initially employs a lighter touch, but once its plucked melodies and reverb-smudged atmospheres give way to a snarling blast of distorted sonics, it’s clear that sts’ primary goal—at least on this record—is to wreak a little havoc.

R A L L Y – Residue (SPE:C)

The so-called “return” of the deep / classic / old-school dubstep aesthetic is routinely framed as a recent phenomenon, but Berlin’s SPE:C label has been proudly carrying the torch for heavy, meditative bassweight for a full decade now. R A L L Y is the latest addition to its artist roster, and if the clattering percussion and patient low-end wobbles that populate his new Residue EP are any indication, the Portland-based artist has spent plenty of time worshipping at the altar of Mala. There’s an inherent spookiness to his productions—the vibe is often akin to walking into an ancient (and possibly haunted) temple—and while he’s got a definite talent for slow motion steppers (“Screen Memory,” “Lup-1N3”), the record never feels sedate. The shuffling drums of opening cut “Zeta Ring” actually verge on UKG territory, adding some welcome pep to the proceedings as R A L L Y plunges into the darkness.

SPF 50 – Ett Inre Rum (Bliss Point)

Words like “deep” and “psychedelic” are often applied to the work of SPF 50, and while the records he’s put out previously have plenty of danceable fare, the NYC-based producer has often gravitated toward wily acid lines and rough-and-tumble rhythms. On the excellent new Ett Inre Rum EP, however, he’s noticeably tightened up his approach, locking into a more hypnotic and stripped-down (albeit still propulsive) strain of techno. Pumping opener “Norrsken” is a standout, and has a bit of post-minimal Robert Hood running through its veins. “Biom” and “Solvind” burrow into the murk, mining the zoned-out bliss one can only find in a high-quality loop, though the latter track then gets a shot in the arm from Erik Luebs, who closes out the record with a remix that employs the same sort of tweaky synths that powered Underworld classics like “Rez” and “Cowgirl.”

Ghost Dubs – Oblique (Pressure)

When it comes to trudging around in the darkest depths of the bass continuum, it’s fair to say that no one feels more comfortable and confident in that particular domain than Kevin Martin (a.k.a. The Bug). Yet the UK veteran does seem to have found a true kindred spirit in Michael Fiedler, a German producer whose own catalog also stretches back several decades. It’s only during the past few years, however, that Fiedler has worked under the name Ghost Dubs, but his decidedly patient approach to subterranean, reverb-soaked rhythm science has proved to be intoxicating. Oblique is his latest full-length, and though it moves with the urgency of a tortoise, its deliberate, static-encrusted rhythms have the gravitational pull of a neutron star, beguiling listeners as Ghost Dubs lumbers his way toward oblivion.

Giulio Aldinucci – Materia (Karlrecords)

Materia is not a small record. Sure, it sounds perfectly adequate coming out of some Bluetooth earbuds or even a pair of tinny laptop speakers, but its thunderous soundscapes are best experienced in a room—preferably an acoustically treated one with a premium soundsystem—where every flutter and tremble can be not just heard, but felt. There’s something visceral about Giulio Aldinucci’s work, and comparisons can easily be drawn to the immersive, borderline punishing output of artists like Tim Hecker and Empytset. Yet Materia, with its sonorous vocal choirs and thunderous drones, is also a beautiful record, and one with a decidedly cinematic bent, recalling both the heavyweight drama of Jóhann Jóhannsson and the mastery of tension and release that Cliff Martinez displayed in his seminal Solaris soundtrack. In other words, somebody in Hollywood would be wise to give this guy a call.

claire rousay & Martyna Basta – hotel room (Unsound)

The seeds of hotel room were sown in 2023, when experimental composers claire rousay and Martyna Basta were brought together by the Unsound festival for a joint residency. Considering that the residency also involved a joint performance, the two artists probably could have banged out an album shortly afterwards. Instead, they elected to let the music they’d created together marinate, continuing the collaboration long distance as they reworked and swapped various drafts and sketches over the course of several years. That patience is reflected in the slow-burning, electroacoustic sprawl of hotel room, most notably in the three tracks that clock in nine minutes or more, but also in its shorter numbers, where twinkling melodies intermingle with weightless drones as ethereal (not to mention heavily processed) vocal tendrils elegantly float through the stereo field.

Clima – Healing Patterns (appendix.files)

Language is a funny thing, and in 2026, the word “healing” has practically become a red flag, more likely to be espoused by some MAHA-pilled ignoramus or pseudoscience-spewing influencer than a medical expert who can provide actual guidance about improving one’s health. But maybe Healing Patterns can help to salvage the term’s reputation. The beguiling, ambient-ish new full-length from Clima, the record sits somewhere between trip-hop, dub techno and a deconstructed strain of IDM, and was apparently created during “a period when chronic illness severely limited the artist’s ability to explore the outside world.” Dealing with that undoubtedly sparked all sorts of frustration—it’s not a coincidence that the closing track is titled “Limitation”—but rather than submitting to darkness, the Berlin-based producer turned toward the light, conjuring up an lush array of free-floating sonics, scattershot rhythms and calmly drifting textures. Could that array actually heal anyone? Maybe not, but at the very least, the album’s blissed-out escapism should offer listeners a welcome bit of relief.

That brings us to the end of today’s First Floor digest. Thank you so much for reading the newsletter, and remember, you can find all of this week’s recommended releases on this handy Buy Music Club list. (If you like them, please buy them.)

Until next time,

Shawn

First Floor is published and overseen by Shawn Reynaldo, a freelance writer, editor, presenter and project manager. Find him on LinkedIn and Instagram—and make sure to follow First Floor on Instagram as well—or you can just drop Shawn an email to get in touch about projects, collaborations or other potential opportunities.

item.title: Siete Catorce Has Better Taste Than I Do
item.description: A guest recommendation from the genre-blurring, speaker-rattling Mexican artist.
item.dc:creator: Shawn Reynaldo
item.content:encoded:
First Floor is in many ways a one-person operation, but on most Wednesdays, the newsletter fully cedes the spotlight to an artist, writer or other figure from the music world, inviting them to recommend a piece of music.

Today’s recommendation comes from Siete Catorce, a Mexican artist who’s now spent more than a decade crafting hybrid Latin rhythms. Born in Mexicali, he spent much of his early life shuttling between the San Francisco Bay Area and the borderlands of Northern Mexico, and that dual existence fostered a musical upbringing in which hip-hop and dubstep ultimately played as big of a role as regional Latin sounds. Connecting the dots between those genres has always been a part of his own work, and long before anyone uttered the phrase “Latin club,” he was turning out adventurous permutations on labels like N.A.A.F.I and Enchufada.

Siete Catorce eventually found his way to Mexico City, but even within the musically rich stew of that sprawling metropolis, he continued to be a one-of-one figure, splicing various strains of techno, bass music, ambient and what might be described as IDM into his upfront productions. (It’s also worth noting that regardless of what genre—or genres—he’s experimenting with at any given moment, high-impact sound design is a major component of his work.) His latest album, El Valle, is another genre-blurring effort, though it does noticeably pull from the canons of cumbia and Mexican tribal. The record is slated to drop later this week as a joint release from Colombian labels Discos Nutabe and In-Correcto, but ahead of its arrival, he’s taken a few moments to dig through his archives and recommended some of his favorite music to First Floor readers. These guest recommendations usually feature a single selection, but Siete Catorce was apparently so inspired that he sent over three; we’ve gone ahead and published them all.

Marcelo Fabian – BEJIA FLOR (UltraPop, 2004)

Trippy, minimal, glitched-out cumbia. I have no idea who this person is—the only track you could find online for a while was a track he did for a ZZK Records cumbia compilation. BEIJA FLOR was shown to me by a friend from Bolivia who said this sounds like me. And it kinda does. But it was made in 2004? It serves as a great reminder that whenever you think you have an original idea in music, somebody probably already made something similar 10 years before.

UPGRAYEDD SMURPHY – #PENINSULA (r-ch-v, 2018)

I saw Smurphy perform this album like 10 times in 2013-2014. It will forever be etched into memory. Every sound, every melody and every kick drum just reminds of how much fun it is to lose yourself on the dancefloor.

CIBER1A – BOZAL (Humidex, 2024)

Crazy tribal broken techno. I love songs that end so far away from where they started and every track on this album is like that. It sounds improvised, but every rhythm makes sense and morphs into what it needs to be. I need more people to listen to this because the keys at the beginning of the second track, “Contraxion,” remind me of something and I need someone to tell me what it is.
